title.narrative: The Human Rights & Social Development Division (HRSD) 2021-2025
The Human Rights & Social Development Division (HRSD) 2021-2025

description.narrative:
Sveriges ambassad i Bangkok föreslår ett nytt stöd till the Human Rights and Social Development Division (HRSD) inom Pacific Community (SPC), för att stödja implementeringen av HRSD:s Business Plan 2021-2025 med ett bidrag om SEK 56 000 000. Det svenska bidraget är ett svar på Sveriges demokratioffensiv (DfD) (regeringsbeslut UD2020/00571) samt bidrar till implementeringen av strategin för Sveriges regionala utvecklingssamarbete i Asien och Oceanien 2016-2021. Inom nuvarande strategi har Sida möjlighet att budgetmässigt förbinda sig fram till och med 2024. Samarbetspartnern uppfyller de juridiska kraven för att ingå ett avtal.
Stödet till HRSD bygger på synergier från de program som de tidigare divisionerna genomfört. HRSD:s Business Plan 2021-2025 har utvecklats för att svara på förändringar i kontexten, inklusive covid-19 pandemins påverkan och klimatkrisen. Planen bygger på samlade erfarenheter från SPC, SPC:s medlemmar, civilsamhället, och andra implementerande partners. Framtagandet har skett genom genom konsultationer, oberoende utvärderingar och granskningar av prioriterade arbetsområden.
En särskild prioritering som det svenska stödet bidrar till är HRSD:s arbete med att integrera jämställdhet och mänskliga rättigheter (HRBA) i allt SPCs arbete, med hjälp av verktyg som P.L.A.N.E.T (Participation, Links to human rights, Accountability, Non-discrimination, Empowerment, Transparency) och People Centered Approach (PCA). HRSD samarbetar med andra tekniska och vetenskapliga avdelningar vid SPC i samfinansierade projekt, samt assisterar fiskeriprogram (så som Sida-stödda PEUMP) och klimatprogram i design, implementering och uppföjning. Insatsen ger ambassaden en strategisk ingångspunkt för att engagera unga människor i Oceanien, vilket är relevant då de är centrala intressenter och drivare av utvecklingsprocesser.
I sitt programförslag har HRSD sammanfattat utvecklingsproblemet i Stillahavsregionen, vilket inkluderar den påverkan som klimatkrisen och covid-19 pandemin har på redan sårbara samhällen. En ökning av människor som lever i fattigdom förutspås, och i flera av samhällets grupper är kvinnor och barn särskilt utsatta. Pandemin har orsakat ett ökat våld mot kvinnor och flickor (VAWG) samtidigt som det sociala skyddsnätet är begränsat. Det finns ett stort behov att stärka en god samhällsstyrning och verka för ett meningsfullt deltagande av det civila samhället för att säkerställa att covid-19-återhämtningen inkluderar såväl sociala dimensioner av hållbarhet som ekonomiska och miljömässiga. Att 'bygga tillbaka bättre' och hitta hållbara lösningar är av högsta relevans. Återkoppling från SPC:s medlemmar visar att regeringar i Oceanien också behöver ökad tillgång till disaggregerad data och statistik för att via sociala trygghetssystem bättre nå människor som lever i särskild utsatthet.

The Embassy proposes a new support to the Human Rights and Social Development Division (HRSD) at the Pacific Community (SPC) to support the implementation of HRSD's Business Plan 2021-2025 with a contribution of SEK 56 000 000, responding to Sweden’s Drive for Democracy (DfD) (government decision UD2020/00571) and the current Strategy of Sweden’s regional development and cooperation in Asia and the Pacific region 2016-2021. The ongoing strategy budget frame can be extended until 2024. The cooperation partner fulfils the legal requirements to enter into an agreement. HRSD is operating under the rules of SPC.
The new HRSD Business Plan 2021-2026 incorporates the RRRT Business Plan 2018-2021 and the SDP Business Plan 2019-2023. The HRSD programme builds on the synergies from these plans, and has adapted in response to the current environment shaped by covid-19 and climate change. The Business Plan draws on insights from across SPC, SPC members, civil society, implementing partners, and evaluators, through consultations, independent evaluations and reviews of work areas.
A key priority which the Swedish funds will cover is the HRSD work on mainstreaming gender and the Human Rights Based Approach (HRBA), using tools as P.L.A.N.E.T (Participation, Links to human rights, Accountability, Non-discrimination, Empowerment, Transparency) and the people-centred approach (PCA) across SPC as an organisation. HRSD engages formally with other technical and scientific divisions at SPC through joint project funding and collaboration, assisting fisheries ( such as Sida- supported PEUMP) programmes and climate change programmes within their programme design, implementation and monitoring. This contribution also gives the embassy a strategic entry point to engage more with young people in the Pacific region. This is assessed to be relevant since they are key stakeholders in development processes.
In the proposal, HRSD has summarized the development problem in the Pacific region, and the drivers of change affecting human rights and social development, including the climate crises and the effect that covid-19 has on already vulnerable economies. A rise in poverty is foreseen, especially for women and young children. The pandemic has also caused an increase in violence against women and girls (VAWG), and limited social services. There is a strong need for good governance and meaningful participation from civil society to ensure that recovery includes social impacts. Post-covid, there is an opportunity to also respond to ecological challenges and the climate crises. There is a need to build back better and find sustainable solutions, especially in the context of temporary and permanent displacement of people. This is both an opportunity and a constraining pressure for members and implementing partners. Feedback from the SPC members suggests that Governments in the Pacific also need disaggregated data and statistics to better target social protection to reach marginalized groups.

The purposes of the HRSD Business Plan are:
• to detail HRSD's key functions and strategies to progress ongoing and emerging human rights and social development priorities in the region; • to detail HRSD's role in supporting SPC to strengthen its people-centred and culturally responsive work; and • to outline transitional activities that HRSD will undergo over its first 12 months as a newly-merged division, and to align with an SPC-wide transition to a new strategic plan.
HRSD's vision is:
"Our vision is for just, equitable and resilient Pacific Island societies. This will be achieved by advancing human rights, gender equality and social inclusion for all Pacific people, grounded in cultural values and principles, and people-centred approaches."
The HRSD Business Plan is built around four objectives, connected to SPCs Development Objective 6 (Advance social development through the promotion of human rights, gender equality, cultural diversity and opportunities for young people):
1. Governance and institutional strengthening: Strengthen inclusive, transparent and responsive governance and institutions for human rights and social development
1.1: State laws, policies and institutions are strengthened to serve the rights of all people
1.2: Civil society (including women and young people) have the capacity and positioning to influence policies and programmes
1.3 Regional leadership improves implementation of human rights and social development priorities at a national level.
2. Equality and social inclusion: Mobilise, empower and build conditions for gender equality and social inclusion in society and development
2.1 Services and programmes target and respond to the needs of the most marginalized (especially in EVAWG, climate change and disaster response).
2.2 Skills and opportunities grow for income generation and sustainable livelihoods among women, young people, artists and cultural producers
2.3 More communities and leaders advocate for human rights, gender equality and non-violence
3. Culture: Promote, preserve and protect positive expressions of culture
3.1 Cultural knowledge is protected and dynamic in development policy/programming
4. Knowledge and innovation: Accelerate the impact of human rights and social development priorities through knowledge, learning and innovative solutions.
4.1 Human rights and social development knowledge is used to inform national policies and development programmes

Special results to highlight from 2025 include:
1. HRSD delivered strong results in 2025, strengthening regional dialogue and public engagement on human rights and gender equality. It convened major events such as the Pacific CEDAW session and expanded outreach through initiatives like the Human Rights Film Festival, increasing awareness across multiple Pacific countries.
2. The division also elevated Pacific leadership globally, particularly in the International Court of Justice climate advisory process. Countries such as Tuvalu, Tonga, and Samoa stood out through active participation, including all-women delegations, ensuring human rights, gender equality, and climate justice perspectives were strongly represented.
3. At national level, HRSD supported concrete policy and institutional progress. This included FSMs UPR submission, Vanuatus first Convention Against Torture report, Fijis Disability Policy (20252030), and the establishment of Tongas Elections Disability Access Working Group. In Solomon Islands, the PYEEEP pilot project enabled 55 young people to access skills development pathways, demonstrating tangible country-level impact.
4. Despite funding challenges, HRSD maintained strong financial oversight and full audit compliance. By prioritising key programmes and strengthening resource mobilisation, it sustained results and continued advancing inclusive governance and long-term institutional change across the region.
For the whole funding period the final report highlights the results achieved under the HRSD Business Plan (20212026), with Sida playing a key strategic role as a "core" partner. Through its funding and partnership, Sida significantly contributed to advancing human rights, gender equality, social inclusion, youth development, and people-centred approaches across the Pacific. Sidas support has enabled both regional and country-level progress by complementing pooled and project-based funding from other partners such as DFAT, MFAT, and SPC. This collaborative financing model is assessed to have strengthened HRSDs ability to deliver integrated programmes and respond to diverse regional priorities. The achievements presented reflect not only HRSDs work but also the collective efforts of Pacific governments, civil society, communities, and development partners. Sidas contribution helped catalyse inclusive, resilient, and locally driven development outcomes across multiple sectors. Overall, Sidas partnership has been instrumental in sustaining the implementation of the HRSD Business Plan, supporting long-term institutional change and reinforcing a coordinated, people-centred development approach in the Pacific region.
Specific results achieved over the program period:
* Strengthened governance, accountability, and implementation systems through policy reform, regional frameworks, and institutional capacity across the Pacific.
* Advanced implementation of international human rights commitments and increased Pacific participation and influence in regional and global mechanisms.
* Expanded inclusion and leadership of women, youth, persons with disabilities, and civil society, while improving access to inclusive services, education, and economic opportunities for marginalised groups.
* Enhanced coordinated, survivor-centred responses to gender-based and technology-facilitated violence, supported by stronger justice systems and services.
* Embedded people-centred, gender-responsive, and rights-based approaches across SPC systems and programmes, while strengthening evidence, learning, and digital governance.
* Elevated Pacific leadership on climate justice, culture, and Indigenous knowledge as drivers of sustainable development and resilience.
* Achieved both immediate outcomes and longer-term institutional change, including stronger national reporting systems, progress toward national human rights institutions, and improved violence response systems.
* Maintained strong operational performance with sound financial management and accountability, positioning HRSDsupported by Sidaas a leading regional platform for inclusive governance and long-term systems change.
Objective specific examples include:
Objective 1. Strengthening Governments and Institutions
HRSD strengthened Pacific leadership and accessibility in the international human rights system by successfully supporting the 2025 Pacific CEDAW Technical Cooperation Sessionthe first of its kind in the region. The initiative engaged 798 participants from 15 Pacific countries, dramatically increasing participation and bringing together governments, civil society, youth, and persons with disabilities. This model shifted treaty engagement from compliance to implementation, accelerating reporting, strengthening follow-up, and enhancing regional cooperation. It also raised global recognition of Pacific-led approaches, influencing international discussions on treaty body reform and demonstrating a more inclusive, participatory, and effective approach to advancing human rights.
Objective 2. Strengthening Civil Society and Rights Holders
Sustained programme support to civil society and rights-based advocacy contributed to a significant legislative reform in Tonga, culminating in the Civil Registration and Digital Identification Act 2025, which raised the legal age of marriage to 18. This result demonstrates how targeted, long-term investments in advocacy and community engagement can drive meaningful policy change and advance the protection of childrens rights.
Social Citizenship Education initiatives reached approximately 38,500 students across the Pacific, promoting gender equality, human rights, inclusion, and violence prevention. Through teacher and community training in Kiribati, expansion in the Marshall Islands, and support to schools in Vanuatu, the programme strengthened local capacity and contributed to long-term behavioural change, addressing the root causes of discrimination, exclusion, and violence.
Objective 3. Advancing Pacific Culture and Cultural Inclusion
Support to VOU Fiji strengthened the role of creative industries as a driver of inclusive economic and social development, generating over 100 jobsaround 60% of which are permanentfor out-of-school youth. The initiative combined accredited skills training with cultural expression, enhancing livelihoods, reinforcing Pacific cultural identity, and demonstrating scalable pathways linking culture, employment, and inclusive development.
Objective 4. Mainstreaming People-Centred Approaches Across SPC
Mainstreaming of people-centred approaches across SPC was significantly strengthened through the PLANET framework (Human Rights Based Approach | Sida), which embedded participation, accountability, and inclusion into institutional systems and programming. By 2025, capacity-building reached staff across eight divisions, with growing demand for gender equality, disability, and cultural inclusion support, and integration into project design processes. This marks a shift from isolated initiatives to systematic, organisation-wide adoption of inclusive, rights-based approaches.
Cross-Cutting Results and Regional Impact
The programme achieved strong cross-cutting, systems-level results by strengthening regional institutions and coordination mechanisms for human rights, governance, gender equality, disability inclusion, youth participation, and cultural development. It reinforced Pacific leadership and ownership in key regional and global processes, including climate justice advocacy and treaty body reform, while promoting culturally grounded approaches. At the same time, it advanced efforts to drive behavioural and social norm change by integrating participatory methods, communications for development, and locally rooted practices, ensuring more sustainable and transformative development outcomes.
Sustainability and Strategic Outlook
The external evaluation (see seperate statement) confirms that HRSD has become a trusted and regionally relevant leader with strong technical credibility and convening power, achieving its most significant results through sustained, long-term, and nationally aligned investments. Moving forward, the division will focus on consolidating these gains by strengthening systems, prioritisation, and delivery models, while deepening country-level impact and institutional change. Key priorities include clearer strategic focus, multi-year country engagement, stronger institutional systems and learning, balanced thematic investment, scaling people-centred approaches, and expanding regional leadershipparticularly in climate justice. Overall, HRSD is well-positioned to sustain impact and partnership with Sida, should new funding opportunities materialize, by reinforcing efficiency, securing more predictable financing, and continuing to deliver inclusive, Pacific-led development outcomes.
The programme has established a strong foundation for continued partnership between Sida and SPC around shared priorities on democratic governance, human rights, gender equality, inclusion, and sustainable Pacific-led development. In recognition of the evolving funding landscape, HRSDs next phase will focus on consolidating results, strengthening efficiency and prioritisation, and adopting risk-mitigating measures through diversified and more predictable financing approaches. This includes positioning HRSD outcomes and regional public goods within broader multi-donor and integrated financing opportunities where strategic alignment exists, including potential future engagement through regional platforms and programmes such as PEUMP II and other complementary funding modalities. Through this approach, HRSD aims to sustain momentum, protect hard-won gains, and continue delivering scalable and long-term development outcomes for Pacific countries and communities while maintaining flexibility to respond to emerging regional priorities.
